Eligibility

Before you apply

Most Malawi residents over 18 can qualify.

We assess affordability, not just a credit score. If you can show stable income and a clear plan for repayment, there is usually a product that fits.

  • Aged 18 or older with a valid national ID or passport
  • Resident in Malawi with a verifiable address
  • Stable income from employment, business or farming
  • Monthly repayment comfortably within your disposable income
  • Business applicants: 6+ months of operation and records

Questions

FAQ

Answers before you apply.

Still unsure? Our help centre covers applications, repayments and account security in more detail.

Visit help centre Call +265 999 123 456
How much can I borrow?

From MWK 50,000 to MWK 80,000,000 depending on the product. Personal loans run to MWK 15 million, business loans to MWK 50 million and secured loans to MWK 80 million. The approved amount is based on affordability.

How long does approval take?

Most complete applications receive a decision within 24 hours. Applications needing document verification or business assessment take 1–3 working days. You can follow every stage in your dashboard.

What documents do I need?

National ID or passport, proof of income and proof of residence. Business applicants also provide business registration and, if available, bank or mobile money statements. Required documents are listed on each product.

Do you charge an application fee?

No. Applying and receiving a decision is free. A processing fee of 1.5–3% applies only if your loan is approved, and it is disclosed before you sign.

Can I repay early?

Yes. Early settlement quotes are available in your dashboard and from support. An early repayment charge of 0–2% of outstanding principal may apply, depending on the product.

What happens if I miss a payment?

Contact us before the due date. We will discuss a payment plan. A late charge applies after five days, and persistent non-payment may be reported to credit reference bureaus.

Who we are

Overview

Local capital, local decisions, local accountability.

We were founded in Lilongwe in 2016 by a small group of credit and agribusiness professionals who were tired of watching good businesses fail for want of a predictable, fairly priced loan.

Today we lend to salaried employees, traders, farmers, cooperatives and growing companies across Malawi. Decisions are made here, by people who understand seasonal income, informal trade and the realities of running a business in a high-cost credit market.

Mission

Make responsible credit simple and accessible.

To provide transparent, affordable credit and practical financial support to Malawian households and businesses, so that borrowing builds opportunity rather than trapping people in debt.

Vision

A Malawi where good ideas can get finance.

To be the most trusted non-bank lender in Malawi — known for fair pricing, human assessment and technology that makes credit easier to understand and manage.

Transparency

Published rates, itemised fees and a total cost figure before you sign. If a charge is not disclosed, it is not payable.

Responsibility

We decline loans we believe are unaffordable and contact customers early when payments slip.

Respect

No pressure, no humiliation, no aggressive recovery. Customers in difficulty are treated with dignity.

Local roots

Malawian staff, Malawian decision-makers, and products designed around how income actually arrives here.

Our history

Ten years of steady growth.

  1. 2016 — Founded in Lilongwe

    Opened with a single office and a focus on salary-based lending for public-sector employees.

  2. 2018 — Business lending launched

    Introduced working-capital loans for registered SMEs and cooperatives, with cash-flow-based assessment.

  3. 2020 — Customer portal

    Launched online statements, repayment tracking and document uploads during the pandemic.

  4. 2022 — Agricultural finance

    Began seasonal lending with harvest-aligned repayment for farmers and agribusinesses.

  5. 2024 — Secured lending and regional reach

    Added secured facilities and expanded field operations to Blantyre, Mzuzu and Zomba.

  6. 2026 — Digital-first lending

    Rebuilt the customer experience around an online application, dashboard, and full fee transparency.

Community

Corporate social responsibility

We reinvest a share of our margin into financial literacy and enterprise support in the communities we lend to.

  • Financial literacy clinics — free monthly sessions on budgeting, saving and borrowing safely, held in Lilongwe, Blantyre and Mzuzu.
  • Women in enterprise — reduced fees and mentoring for women-led small businesses in their first two years.
  • Agribusiness partnerships — input financing and record-keeping training with farmer cooperatives.
  • School fees bridge — short-term facilities timed to school terms, with budgeting support for parents.
  • Digital access — low-bandwidth pages and USSD-style support for customers without smartphones.

Ask about the next clinic at hello@jaycobfinancial.mw.

Total repayment—

Flat rate explained

Interest is charged on the full principal for the whole term, even as the balance falls. It is simpler to calculate but costs more in total.

Reducing balance explained

Interest is charged on the balance you still owe each period. As the balance falls, the interest portion of each instalment falls too.

What is APR?

The annual percentage rate expresses the total cost of credit — interest plus disclosed fees — as a yearly rate, so products can be compared fairly.

Borrowing costs money. This calculator is an estimate, not an offer of credit. Only the signed loan agreement is binding. If you are struggling with debt, read our Responsible Lending Policy or call us before taking on more credit.
Home/How it works
Ten steps · no surprises

How it works

From creating your account to your final repayment, here is exactly what happens, how long it takes and what we need from you at each stage.

Create an account Check eligibility
1–10 minutes account and application 1 working day document verification 1–3 days credit assessment Same day – 48 hrs disbursement after signing

Step 1

Create your account

Register with your name, date of birth, national ID number, phone number and email address. Choose a strong password and accept the terms and privacy policy.

What you need: email or phone number, national ID, date of birth.

Timing: 2 minutes.

Create an account

Step 2

Verify your email and phone

We send a six-digit one-time code by SMS and email. Enter it to activate your account. Codes expire after 10 minutes and can be resent once every 60 seconds.

What you need: access to your phone and inbox.

Timing: under a minute.

Step 3

Choose your loan product

Compare limits, terms, rates and fees on the products page. Use the calculator to test instalments and total cost, then pick the product that fits your need and cash flow.

Tip: shorter terms cost less interest but need a larger instalment.

Compare products

Step 4

Run the numbers

Use the calculator to see the instalment, total interest, fees and full schedule. Save or print the estimate so you can compare it with your budget.

Tip: aim to keep total debt repayments below 40% of net income.

Open the calculator

Step 5

Complete the application

Five guided steps: loan details, personal and employment information, business and bank details, documents, and a final review. You get a reference number on submission and can save a draft at any point.

What you need: ID, income evidence, residence proof, bank or mobile money details.

Start an application

Step 6

Document verification

Our team checks that your ID, income evidence and residence proof are legible, current and consistent with your application. If something is missing or unclear we tell you exactly what to replace.

Timing: usually within one working day.

Step 7

Credit and affordability assessment

We review income, expenses, existing obligations and credit conduct, and may check with credit reference bureaus with your consent. Where affordability is marginal we may offer a smaller amount or a longer term.

Timing: 1–3 working days after documents are complete.

Step 8

Decision and agreement

You receive an approval, an approval with conditions, a request for more information, or a decline with reasons. If approved, the agreement shows the amount, rate, fees, schedule and total cost of credit.

Tip: read the agreement and the fee disclosure before signing.

Step 9

Disbursement

Once the agreement is signed, funds are paid to the bank or mobile money account verified in your name — usually the same day, and within 48 hours at the latest. You receive a disbursement notification and receipt.

What you need: an account in your own name and a signed agreement.

Step 10

Repay and monitor

    KYC requirements

    Criteria explained

    How we decide.

    Affordability

    Verified income minus essential expenses must comfortably cover the instalment. We aim for total debt repayments below 40% of net income.

    Identity & residency

    You must be 18+, resident in Malawi with a verifiable address, and able to produce valid identification.

    Credit conduct

    Existing arrears, defaults or frequent missed payments reduce affordability. A clean record or cleared arrears helps.

    Ability to document

    Complete, legible documents speed up decisions. Missing documents are the most common reason for delays.

    We may still say no. Every application is individually assessed. We decline applications we believe are unaffordable, even where the preliminary score is strong. Read our Responsible Lending Policy.

    *APR is indicative and includes interest plus the disclosed processing fee, expressed as an annual rate. It assumes the loan runs to term with no late payments. Your actual APR is shown in your pre-contract disclosure and agreement.

    What APR means

    The annual percentage rate shows the yearly cost of credit including interest and disclosed fees. It lets you compare a 24% loan with a 2% fee against a 22% loan with a 4% fee on equal terms.

    Why rates differ

    Unsecured lending carries more risk than secured lending, short terms need faster capital recovery, and a stronger credit record earns better pricing.

    Fixed for the term

    The rate in your agreement does not change during the term. Changes to our published rates apply only to new agreements.

    Help centre

    Frequently asked questions.

    How do I check the status of my application?

    Sign in and open My loan applications. Each application shows its stage — pending, under review, information required, approved, rejected or withdrawn — plus reviewer comments and any outstanding documents.

    What does “information required” mean?

    We need something from you before we can decide — usually a clearer document, a payslip or an explanation. The application page lists exactly what is needed, with an upload or respond action.

    Why was my application declined?

    The most common reasons are affordability (the instalment is too high relative to income), incomplete documents, or a poor credit record. The decision message gives the reason. You can reapply after addressing it.

    How long does disbursement take?

    Usually the same working day after a signed agreement, and within 48 hours at the latest. Mobile money is often faster than bank transfer. You receive a disbursement notification with a receipt.

    Can I change my repayment date?

    In some cases. Ask support at least three working days before the due date. A change may affect the schedule and any accrued interest, and a restructuring fee may apply.

    How do I get a statement?

    Open Account statements in the dashboard, choose the account and period, and download or print. Statements cover loans, savings and wallet activity and carry a verification reference.

    How do I close my account?

    Loans must be settled first. Then request closure in Settings → Account closure. We confirm in writing, retain records required by law, and delete the rest in line with our retention policy.

    How do I complain?

    Use the contact form above with the category “Complaint”, email complaints@jaycobfinancial.mw, or call. You get a ticket reference, an acknowledgement within two working days and a substantive response within 15 working days.

    How we detect and report money laundering, fraud and terrorist financing.

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. Our obligation

    As a regulated lender we must monitor transactions, screen customers and report suspicious activity to the Financial Intelligence Authority. We do not tell customers when a report has been made, as the law prohibits tipping off.

    2. Customer due diligence

    We identify and verify every customer, identify beneficial owners of corporate borrowers, screen against sanctions and politically exposed person lists, and apply enhanced due diligence to higher-risk relationships.

    We may ask for source-of-funds information, additional identification, or evidence of the purpose of a loan.

    3. Monitoring

    Transactions are monitored for unusual size, frequency, round amounts, rapid disbursement and repayment patterns, mismatches with stated purpose, and use of accounts not in the customer’s name.

    An alert does not mean you have done anything wrong. We investigate and may contact you for an explanation.

    4. Prohibited conduct

    We do not lend for illegal activity, do not accept third-party repayments without verification, and will not process transactions connected to sanctioned persons or entities.

    5. Reporting and records

    Suspicious activity reports are filed with the Financial Intelligence Authority. Records of customer due diligence, monitoring alerts and reports are kept for at least five years.

    Questions about this document?Email support@jaycobfinancial.mw or call +265 999 123 456. You can also raise a formal complaint through our complaints process.

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. How to complain

    Raise a complaint in the dashboard under Support → Complaint submission, email complaints@jaycobfinancial.mw, call +265 999 123 456 or write to Plot 47/3, Area 47, Sector 3, Lilongwe.

    Tell us what happened, when, what you want us to do and your preferred contact method. Attach any supporting documents. You will receive a ticket reference immediately.

    2. Our process

    Acknowledgement within 2 working days. Investigation and a substantive response within 15 working days for most complaints, or 30 working days where third parties or complex records are involved. We will keep you updated if we need longer.

    If we uphold your complaint we will explain the remedy, correct our records and, where relevant, refund charges or correct credit bureau data.

    3. Escalation

    If you are unhappy with our final response, or we have not responded within the stated period, you may ask for a review by our Complaints Officer and then escalate to the Reserve Bank of Malawi consumer protection unit or the relevant financial services regulator.

    You can also seek independent legal advice or mediation. Escalation does not affect your legal rights and we will not penalise you for complaining.

    4. Payment disputes

    Report a missing or misapplied payment from My transactions → Report a missing payment. Include the mobile money or bank reference. We reconcile within 3 working days and correct any error with interest adjustment where appropriate.

    5. Records

    We keep a complaint register, recording the issue, our response, the outcome and any remedy, for regulatory review and service improvement.

    Questions about this document?Email support@jaycobfinancial.mw or call +265 999 123 456. You can also raise a formal complaint through our complaints process.

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. Consent at application

    By submitting an application you confirm that the information is accurate and consent to identity verification, affordability and credit assessment, sharing with credit reference bureaus, and processing of your data as described in the Privacy Policy.

    You consent to service communications by email, SMS and in-app notification. Marketing consent is separate, optional and unticked by default.

    2. Recording consent

    Each consent is timestamped and linked to the application reference. Security-sensitive actions such as transfers require a fresh one-time code.

    3. Withdrawing consent

    Withdraw marketing consent in Settings → Notification preferences or by replying STOP to an SMS. Withdraw other consents by contacting us; where processing is necessary for a live loan or legal obligation, we will explain why it must continue.

    4. Retention periods

    Application data for declined or withdrawn applications: 24 months. Active loan records: the life of the loan plus 6 years. KYC and AML records: at least 5 years after the relationship ends. Complaints: 5 years. Marketing preferences: until withdrawn plus 12 months.

    When a period ends, records are securely deleted or irreversibly anonymised for statistics.

    5. Your choices

    Request a copy, correction, deletion or portability of your data from Settings → Privacy and data requests. We respond within 30 days and explain any legal limitation.

    Before you write to us

    What happens after I submit the form?

    Is the first consultation really free?

    1. What we use

    Strictly necessary cookies and browser storage keep you signed in, remember your security preferences and protect forms against cross-site request forgery. The site does not work without these.

    Analytics storage helps us understand which pages are used so we can improve them. Marketing storage is used only where you opt in.

    2. Local storage in this demonstration

    Because this is a static demonstration, account data, applications, notifications and preferences are stored in your browser’s local storage under keys beginning with jcob_. Nothing is transmitted to a server.

    Clearing site data removes your demo account and loan records. You can reset the demonstration data at any time from Settings.

    3. Third parties

    Fonts are loaded from Google Fonts, which receives your IP address as part of the request. Payment, SMS and analytics providers may set their own cookies when those integrations are enabled.

    4. Managing cookies

    You can block or delete cookies and site data in your browser settings. Blocking strictly necessary storage will prevent sign-in and applications from working.

    Where consent is required, a banner records your choice and you can change it later from Settings → Privacy.

    1. What we share

    With your consent, we may share your identity details, the type and amount of credit, repayment performance, arrears and default status with licensed credit reference bureaus.

    We share only accurate, up-to-date data and update bureaus when a balance changes, a dispute is resolved or an account is closed.

    2. What we receive

    Credit bureau reports help us assess affordability and existing obligations. We also use them to verify identity and detect fraud.

    3. Your credit record

    A late payment, arrears or default can stay on your record for several years and may affect future borrowing, employment checks or tenancy applications. Paying on time builds a positive record.

    You can request a free copy of your credit report from a licensed bureau and challenge inaccurate entries.

    4. Correcting errors

    If you believe we have reported something incorrectly, raise it in Settings → Privacy and data requests or email credit@jaycobfinancial.mw. We investigate within 15 working days and correct the bureau record where we find an error.

    If you disagree with our finding you can add a statement of dispute to your record.

    5. Consent

    You give consent to credit checks during the application, and that consent is recorded with the application reference. You can withdraw consent for future checks, though this may prevent us from lending to you.

    1. Your rights

    To be treated fairly, with dignity and without discrimination. To clear, timely information in a language you understand. To privacy and protection of your data. To a copy of your agreement, schedule and statements.

    To know the full cost of credit before signing. To withdraw an application before disbursement. To repay early. To complain and to receive a reasoned response. To access your credit record and correct errors.

    2. Our commitments

    We disclose rates, fees and total cost in writing. We assess affordability before lending. We respond to support requests within one working day and complaints within the published timescales.

    We provide accessible communication and reasonable adjustments for disability, illness or caring responsibilities.

    3. Your responsibilities

    Provide accurate information and tell us when circumstances change. Keep your contact details current. Protect your password, PIN and one-time codes. Read the agreement before signing.

    Pay on time, or contact us early if you cannot. Do not use loan funds for unlawful purposes. Tell us immediately about suspected fraud on your account.

    4. Accessible banking

    Our site supports keyboard navigation, screen readers, visible focus states and high-contrast text. If any part is difficult to use, tell us and we will provide the information another way.

    5. Fair treatment

    No customer is disadvantaged because of age, gender, disability, marital status, ethnicity, religion, HIV status or political opinion. Lending decisions are based on affordability and credit assessment only.

    Data Protection Policy

    Our internal standards for lawful, fair and secure processing of customer data.

    Policies

    • Privacy policy
    • Terms & conditions
    • Loan agreement terms
    • Cookie policy
    • Responsible lending
    • Complaints & disputes
    • Data protection
    • KYC & identification
    • AML & counter-terrorism
    • Credit reporting
    • Fees & charges
    • Customer rights
    • Consent & retention
    • Licensing disclosure

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. Principles

    We process personal data lawfully, fairly and transparently; collect only what we need; keep it accurate; retain it only as long as necessary; and protect it with appropriate technical and organisational measures.

    Sensitive identifiers such as national ID numbers, account numbers and financial balances are masked by default in the interface and in exports.

    2. Lawful bases

    We rely on contract performance for loan administration, legal obligation for KYC and AML records, legitimate interests for fraud prevention and service improvement, and consent for marketing and optional data uses.

    Where consent is the basis, you can withdraw it at any time without affecting processing already carried out.

    3. Access control

    Access is role-based and least-privilege. Staff access to customer records is logged. Administrative actions require elevated rights and are reviewed.

    Data is encrypted in transit and at rest. Backups are protected and tested. Devices used by staff require screen locks and encryption.

    4. Third parties and transfers

    Processors are appointed under written agreements with confidentiality, security and audit obligations. Cross-border transfers occur only where adequate protection exists or the customer has consented.

    5. Breach response

    6. Requests

    Access, correction, deletion, restriction, portability and objection requests are handled within 30 days. Submit them in Settings → Privacy and data requests or email privacy@jaycobfinancial.mw.

    Agribusiness8 min read9 August 2026

    Financing a season: cash-flow planning for smallholder agribusiness

    Inputs in November, revenue in June. A practical framework for surviving the gap without expensive emergency credit.

    JB By Jay C. O. Banda, Founder & Lead Financial Planner 9 August 2026

    A farming season is not a monthly business. Inputs are bought in one lump, labour is paid in bursts, and revenue arrives months later, often all at once. A budget that treats every month the same will run out of money in February — precisely when the crop needs one more pass.

    Start with the cash calendar, not the crop budget

    List every month of the season down the left of a page. Across the top, put four columns: opening cash, money in, money out, closing cash. Then fill it honestly, using last season's records and this season's prices. Most farmers discover two things immediately: the lowest cash month (usually January to March), and the size of the gap they need to bridge.

    That gap has a number. If it is MWK 400,000, you can plan for MWK 400,000. If it is vague, you will borrow at the worst possible moment at the worst possible terms.

    Separate the three costs

    • Direct inputs — seed, fertiliser, chemicals, hired labour for land prep and harvest.
    • Fixed overheads — land rent, equipment maintenance, permits, storage, family drawings.
    • Financing costs — interest, fees, and the cost of any delayed payment.

    Most smallholder budgets track only the first. The second and third are what turn a profitable season into a break-even one. Include them before you decide a crop is worth planting.

    Price the season at three yields

    Build the plan at your expected yield, then at 70% of it, then at 50%. If the business only works at the optimistic number, the structure is too fragile. Look at what changes: can you reduce hired labour? Plant a shorter-cycle crop on part of the land? Contract storage in advance at a fixed rate rather than paying spot prices in a shortage?

    The goal is not to predict the season. It is to build something that survives a bad one.

    Structure credit to the harvest, not to the calendar

    Short-term facilities priced monthly can be brutal when they are taken for a six-month production cycle. Ask three questions before signing:

    1. What is the all-in cost? Interest plus fees plus any compulsory insurance or savings requirement, expressed as a single figure for the whole period.
    2. When is repayment due? If the first instalment lands before your harvest, the facility is mis-structured for your cycle.
    3. What happens if the harvest is late? A rollover or grace period is worth more than a marginally lower rate.

    Where possible, match repayment to the buyer's payment terms. A contract with an off-taker who pays in July should not be financed by a facility that demands money in April.

    Buy inputs early; buy them in writing

    Input prices tend to move against the buyer as the season approaches. Pre-season purchase, group buying through a cooperative, or an agreed forward price with a supplier all reduce the cash spike. Get the agreement in writing, including delivery dates and replacement terms for defective stock. Verbal promises are not a supply chain.

    Keep a reserve — even a small one

    Target 10% of the season's total cost held in reserve. It sounds impossible in a tight year. Start at 3% and build. The reserve is not idle money; it is what stops a small problem — a pump failure, a delayed delivery, a funeral — from becoming an emergency loan at 30% a month.

    Record the season while it is happening Bags harvested, bags sold, price per bag, labour paid, transport paid. Ten minutes a week. Next season's plan is only as good as this season's records, and lenders who see two years of records treat you as a different class of borrower.

    When to seek advice

    If the cash calendar shows a gap you cannot cover, or if a lender's repayment schedule does not line up with your harvest, get a second opinion before you sign. Restructuring a facility is far easier before it goes into arrears than after.

    Budgeting6 min read12 September 2026

    The 50/30/20 budget, recalculated for a Malawian salary

    Why the imported rule of thumb needs adjusting for transport, family support and seasonal income — and what to use instead.

    TM By Thandiwe Mwale, Head of Credit Advisory 12 September 2026

    The 50/30/20 rule is a decent starting point and a poor finishing point. It assumes a payslip that arrives on the same date every month, transport that costs a predictable amount, and a household that pays for itself. For a great many Malawian earners, none of those three things are reliably true.

    What the rule actually says

    Popularised by US senator Elizabeth Warren, the framework splits take-home pay into three buckets: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and debt repayment. It is memorable, which is why it travels. But it was designed around a high-income, low-volatility household in a country with a stable currency and a functioning consumer-credit market.

    Here is the problem. If rent, transport, food and electricity already consume 68% of your net pay, telling you to cap needs at 50% is not advice. It is arithmetic you cannot perform. The rule is not wrong so much as incomplete.

    Recalculate for four local realities

    1. Transport is a need, and it is not small

    For many Lilongwe and Blantyre commuters, minibus fares or fuel absorb 15–25% of net income. That belongs in the needs bucket, not the wants bucket. If you are spending MWK 60,000 a month getting to work in order to earn MWK 400,000, your true "needs floor" is structurally higher than any imported template allows.

    2. Family support is a fixed obligation, not a leak

    School fees for a younger sibling, a parent's medication, a rural home's inputs — these are commitments, often made before the salary arrives. Build them into the plan as a named line item. Budgets fail when they treat generosity as an accident.

    3. Income is seasonal, so the budget must be annual

    If you earn from farming, contract work, tourism or informal trade, a monthly budget will lie to you. Budget the year, then divide. Work out total expected annual income, total committed annual costs, and the amount you need to set aside in strong months to survive weak ones.

    4. Inflation changes the target every quarter

    A budget built in January may be unworkable by July. Revisit the food, fuel and transport lines quarterly, and raise your savings contribution with your income rather than waiting for a "good month".

    A budget is not a restriction. It is a decision made in advance, by you, when you are calm — instead of at the till, when you are not.

    A workable alternative: the four-account method

    Instead of three percentages, use four accounts and a sequence. This works with a mobile money wallet and one bank account.

    1. Commitments account. Rent, school fees, utilities, family support, loan instalments. Fund this first, on payday, before anything else moves.
    2. Living account. Food, transport, airtime, household consumables. Fund it weekly if you find monthly lump sums disappear too quickly.
    3. Buffer account. A small, boring emergency fund held somewhere you cannot tap instantly. Target one month of commitments, then three.
    4. Future account. Savings, investments and extra debt repayment. Whatever remains after the first three are funded goes here — and the percentage will vary month to month, which is fine.

    What to do with the percentages

    If you want a rule, use this one: commitments under 55%, living under 30%, buffer and future at least 15%. If commitments are already above 55%, your first project is not budgeting — it is reducing fixed costs or raising income. A spreadsheet cannot solve a structural shortfall, and pretending otherwise is how people end up blaming themselves for arithmetic.

    Try this on payday Move the commitments total out of your salary account within 24 hours of being paid. Automate it if your bank allows standing orders. Money that stays in one account tends to get spent once, twice, and then borrowed against.

    Track three numbers, not thirty

    Most people abandon tracking because the spreadsheet is too detailed. You only need three numbers each week: money in, money out, and the gap. Write them on a wall calendar if that is what it takes. After two months you will see the pattern — and the pattern is the point.

    If you want a second pair of eyes, bring three months of statements to a Money Clarity Session. We will build the four accounts with you and tell you honestly whether the problem is spending, structure, or income.

    SME finance7 min read28 August 2026

    Seven documents that decide your SME loan application

    Lenders rarely reject a good business. They reject an incomplete file. Here is the paperwork that moves you to the front of the queue.

    CP By Chikondi Phiri, SME Finance Specialist 28 August 2026

    In most rejections we review, the business is viable. The file is not. A credit officer has roughly twenty minutes to understand your business, assess risk, and justify a decision to a committee. Your documents are doing the arguing for you — or failing to.

    1. Twelve months of bank statements, in the business name

    This is the most common avoidable failure. If business takings run through a personal wallet or a joint account with school fees and rent, the lender cannot separate trading performance from household spending. Open a dedicated business account, route all sales through it, and keep personal transfers clearly labelled. Do that for six months before applying and your assessed turnover changes materially.

    Print the statements. Highlight the salary you pay yourself, if any. Lenders are not suspicious of an owner being paid — they are suspicious of an owner who cannot show how much.

    2. Management accounts, not just year-end financials

    Year-end accounts tell a lender what happened up to eighteen months ago. Management accounts — a simple profit and loss plus a balance sheet, monthly, reconciled — tell them what is happening now. You do not need software. A spreadsheet with consistent categories, updated monthly, is enough. Inconsistency is the killer: if "transport" means fuel in one month and a vehicle purchase in another, the numbers are not comparable.

    3. A 12-month cash-flow forecast you can defend

    Most rejected forecasts are too optimistic and too round. A credible forecast states its assumptions: expected volume growth, price changes, debtor days, stock turn, and the timing of any seasonal dip. If your business is seasonal, show the trough and show how the facility covers it. Lenders are far more comfortable with a forecast that anticipates a hard month than with one that assumes smooth growth.

    A lender is not buying your optimism. They are buying evidence that you understand your own cash cycle.

    4. Six months of supplier and customer evidence

    Invoices, purchase orders, contracts, delivery notes, or a mobile money merchant statement. The purpose is proof of a trading relationship that existed before the loan. Three repeat customers with documented monthly orders are more persuasive than a list of forty prospects.

    5. A debt schedule — including informal debt

    List every facility: bank loans, mobile loans, supplier credit, family loans, hire purchase. Include the monthly instalment and the outstanding balance. Undisclosed obligations discovered later are treated as a misrepresentation, even when the omission was casual. If you are heavily leveraged, say so and bring the plan to reduce it; hiding it ends the conversation permanently.

    6. Identification, registration and tax compliance

    Certificate of incorporation or business registration, TIN, recent tax returns or a compliance letter, directors' IDs and proof of address. These are unglamorous and they stop a file dead. Check the expiry dates. A file that is complete but for a lapsed document sits in a queue until somebody notices, and by then your season has moved on.

    7. A one-page summary that a committee can read

    Attach a short cover sheet: what the business does, what the money is for, how much is needed, the repayment source, and the primary risk with your mitigation. Keep it to one page. The credit officer will use it to brief the committee. Give them a clean sentence and you have influenced the meeting you were not invited to.

    What "loan-ready" actually looks like

    Our rule of thumb: a lender should be able to approve you without asking a single clarifying question. If they have to call you for statements, the application loses a week; if they have to call twice, it often loses momentum altogether.

    Before you submit Read your own file as if you were the credit officer, and ask one question: "Would I lend to this business on this evidence?" If the honest answer is "not yet", you already know what to fix.

    If you would rather have the file reviewed before it goes in, the Loan Readiness Sprint covers exactly that: statements, credit profile, affordability, document pack and lender matching. It is considerably cheaper than a declined application on your record.

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. Why we verify

    Know-your-customer checks confirm you are who you say you are, prevent identity fraud, and meet anti-money-laundering obligations. We cannot disburse a loan until verification is complete.

    2. What we accept

    Primary identity: a valid Malawian national ID card, passport or driving licence. Documents must be current, legible, show the photo and number, and match the name on the application.

    Proof of residence: a utility bill, tenancy agreement, bank or mobile money statement, or a letter from a local authority dated within the last three months.

    Proof of income: payslips for the last three months, an employer letter, business bank or mobile money statements, or audited accounts for larger businesses.

    3. Liveness and matching

    We may request a selfie or short video to confirm identity, and we cross-check names, dates of birth and ID numbers against the documents supplied and, where relevant, credit bureau records.

    On a mismatch we ask for clarification rather than automatically declining. Repeated mismatches or suspected forgery are escalated and may be reported.

    4. Document statuses

    In your dashboard each document shows Approved, Pending, Rejected or Expired. Rejected documents include the reason and a replace action. Expired documents trigger a reminder before they lapse.

    5. Retention and security

    Identity records are retained for at least five years after the end of the relationship, as required for AML purposes, and are stored encrypted with restricted access.

    You can view, download and correct your KYC record. Deletion requests are limited where retention is legally required; we will explain any limitation.

    1. The facility

    The agreement records the principal amount in Malawi Kwacha (MWK), the annual interest rate, the interest method (flat or reducing balance), the repayment frequency (monthly or fortnightly), the number of instalments, the first due date and the maturity date.

    The approved amount may differ from the amount requested. Disbursement is made to the bank or mobile money account verified in your name.

    2. Interest and fees

    Interest accrues from the disbursement date at the agreed annual rate, calculated on the agreed method. A processing fee, and where applicable an administration fee, is disclosed in the Fee Disclosure Statement and deducted or invoiced as stated.

    Rates, fees and charges are fixed for the term shown in the agreement. Any future variation applies only to new agreements, unless the agreement expressly provides otherwise.

    3. Repayment

    Instalments fall due on the dates in the repayment schedule. Each instalment is applied first to charges then interest then principal, unless the agreement states otherwise.

    You may repay early. Early settlement figures are quoted on request and in your dashboard; an early repayment charge may apply as disclosed. Partial prepayments reduce principal and may shorten the term.

    4. Late payment and default

    A late payment charge applies to overdue instalments as set out in the Fee Disclosure Statement. We will contact you by SMS, email and in-app notification before and after a due date.

    Persistent non-payment is a default. On default we may demand the outstanding balance, apply default interest, report the account to credit reference bureaus, recover through guarantors or collateral where applicable, and take lawful recovery action. We will always try to agree a restructure first.

    5. Security, guarantors and insurance

    Secured loans require the collateral described in the agreement and its schedule. Guarantors confirm they understand their obligations and consent to their details being verified.

    Credit life or property insurance is optional unless the agreement states it is a condition. Any insurance premium is disclosed separately from interest.

    6. Statements and notices

    Statements are available in your dashboard and by request. Notices are sent to the email address and phone number on record; you must tell us when those change.

    The agreement is governed by Malawian law. Copies, including a signed version, are provided to you and retained by us for the periods required by law.

    Financial data: income, expenses, existing debt obligations, employer or business details, bank or mobile money details, loan applications, repayment history and transaction records.

    Verification data: copies of identification, proof of income, proof of residence, business registration documents and photographs you upload.

    Technical data: IP address, device and browser type, pages visited, session timestamps and security logs, collected to keep your account safe.

    3. Why we use your data

    To verify your identity and meet know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering obligations.

    To assess affordability and credit risk, including through credit reference bureaus where you have consented.

    To administer loans, process disbursements and repayments, generate statements and provide customer support.

    To detect and prevent fraud, secure accounts and comply with lawful requests from regulators or courts.

    To send service messages by email, SMS and in-app notification. Marketing messages are sent only where you have opted in and can be switched off in Settings at any time.

    4. Sharing

    We share data with service providers who help us operate: payment and mobile money partners, credit reference bureaus, identity verification providers, hosting and communication providers, auditors and professional advisers. Each is bound by confidentiality and data-processing obligations.

    We may disclose information to the Reserve Bank of Malawi, law enforcement or other authorities where the law requires it, and to a purchaser or successor in the event of a corporate transaction.

    We never sell your personal data.

    5. Your rights

    You can request access to the personal data we hold, ask us to correct it, request deletion where we no longer have a lawful basis to keep it, object to certain processing, and withdraw marketing consent.

    Requests can be made from Settings → Privacy and data requests in your dashboard, or by emailing privacy@jaycobfinancial.mw. We respond within 30 days and may ask you to verify your identity first.

    6. Security and retention

    Data is encrypted in transit, access is limited to staff who need it, and sensitive identifiers are masked in screens, exports and notifications. We keep records only for as long as required for the loan relationship, regulatory record-keeping and dispute resolution.

    If a breach affects your rights, we will notify you and the relevant authority without undue delay.

    Questions about this document?Email support@jaycobfinancial.mw or call +265 999 123 456. You can also raise a formal complaint through our complaints process.

    Responsible Lending Policy

    How we lend affordably, what we will never do, and how to get help if you are struggling.

    Policies

    • Privacy policy
    • Terms & conditions
    • Loan agreement terms
    • Cookie policy

    Version 3.0 · Last updated 1 October 2026 · Applies to all customers in Malawi

    1. Our commitment

    We lend only where the evidence shows you can repay without hardship. Affordability assessment considers verified income, essential living costs, existing debt and the proposed instalment.

    We do not use aggressive recovery tactics, we do not pressure customers into refinancing, and we do not lend to anyone we believe cannot afford the repayments.

    2. Affordability assessment

    We look at disposable income after essential expenses, the total cost of credit, your repayment history and any signs of financial difficulty. As a guide, total debt repayments should stay below 40% of net monthly income.

    Where affordability is marginal we may offer a smaller amount, a longer term, a different product or suggest a savings plan first.

    3. Transparency

    Before you sign, you receive the amount, rate, fees, total cost of credit, repayment schedule and the consequences of late payment in writing. There are no hidden charges.

    Calculator outputs and eligibility results are estimates. Only the signed agreement is binding.

    4. If you are struggling

    Contact us before you miss a payment. We can discuss a payment plan, a restructure, a short payment holiday where policy allows, or referral to a debt counselling service.

    Never borrow from a third party to pay another lender without advice. Tell us if you are dealing with multiple lenders — we can help you prioritise essentials.

    5. Vulnerable customers

    We take extra care with customers experiencing bereavement, illness, job loss, domestic abuse or mental health difficulties. Tell us and we will adapt how we communicate and give you time to respond.

    6. Complaints

    If we get responsible lending wrong, complain. Our Complaints and Dispute Resolution Policy explains timescales and escalation, including to the Reserve Bank of Malawi consumer protection unit.

    Questions about this document?Email support@jaycobfinancial.mw or call +265 999 123 456. You can also raise a formal complaint through our complaints process.

    Our method

    The same four steps, whatever the brief.

    Structure is what makes advice repeatable. Every mandate follows the sequence below, with a written deliverable at each stage.

    48hTypical response time to a new enquiry
    10 daysAverage time to a signed-off plan

    Understand

    A structured discovery session covering income, obligations, goals and constraints — plus the documents behind them.

    Diagnose

    We model the current position, stress-test it, and identify the two or three levers that will actually change the outcome.

    Recommend

    A written plan with options, costs and trade-offs. You approve the route before any application or product is touched.

    Deliver

    We execute alongside you — drafting, chasing, negotiating — then review progress on a fixed calendar.

    Questions

    Before you book

    A few things clients usually ask on the first call.

    How quickly can we start?

    Discovery calls are usually available within three working days. Most engagements begin within a week of that call, once the scope and fee are confirmed in writing.

    Do you charge for the first meeting?

    No. The first 30-minute discovery call is free. If we are not the right fit, we will tell you there and point you elsewhere where we can.

    Are you tied to a particular bank or insurer?

    No. We work with a range of licensed institutions and disclose any referral arrangement before you instruct us. We are not paid by lenders to place business.

    Can you help if I am outside Lilongwe?

    Yes. Roughly half of our clients are outside Lilongwe and work with us by phone, WhatsApp and video. We also run monthly clinics in Kasungu, Salima and Mulanje.

    What if I have already been declined?

    That is one of the most common starting points. We review the decision, identify what drove it, and build a realistic remediation plan rather than simply resubmitting.

    Do you offer services in Chichewa?

    Yes. Sessions can be conducted in English or Chichewa, and we can arrange Yao or Tumbuka interpretation for group workshops with notice.

    Start the conversation

    Not sure which service fits?

    Describe the situation in plain language and we will point you to the right scope — even if the answer is that you do not need us yet.

    1. Acceptance

    By using this website or the customer dashboard you agree to these terms, our Privacy Policy and any product-specific terms presented during an application. If you do not agree, please do not use the service.

    This is a demonstration environment. No real credit is advanced, no money is moved and all figures, decisions and reference numbers are illustrative.

    2. Eligibility and accounts

    You must be at least 18 years old, resident in Malawi and legally able to enter into a credit agreement. You must provide accurate, current information and keep it up to date.

    You are responsible for keeping your password, one-time codes and devices secure, and for all activity carried out under your credentials. Tell us immediately if you suspect unauthorised access.

    3. Credit decisions

    Every application is subject to identity verification, document checks, affordability assessment and credit assessment. We may approve, approve with conditions, request further information, decline or offer a different amount or term.

    Indicative figures on this site, including calculator outputs and eligibility results, are estimates and do not constitute an offer of credit. A binding agreement arises only when a loan agreement is signed by both parties and funds are disbursed.

    4. Acceptable use

    You may not use the service to submit false information or forged documents, attempt to access another person’s account, interfere with the security or availability of the platform, scrape content at scale or use the service for unlawful purposes.

    We may suspend or close an account, and report suspected fraud, where these rules are broken.

    5. Availability and liability

    We aim to keep the service available but do not guarantee uninterrupted access. Maintenance, connectivity, mobile network availability and third-party services may cause downtime.

    To the extent permitted by Malawian law, we are not liable for indirect or consequential loss arising from use of the website. Nothing in these terms limits liability that cannot lawfully be excluded, including for fraud.

    6. Changes and governing law

    We may update these terms; material changes are announced in the dashboard and take effect 30 days after publication. Continued use after that date means acceptance.

    These terms are governed by the laws of Malawi and disputes are handled under our Complaints and Dispute Resolution Policy before any court action.

    Questions about this document?Email support@jaycobfinancial.mw or call +265 999 123 456. You can also raise a formal complaint through our complaints process.
